title: Exact theory of chirality-dependent p-wave magnetism and Edelstein effect in spin spirals
authors: Börge Göbel, Tom G. Saunderson, Freia Opfermann, Lennart Schimpf, Ersoy Şaşıoğlu, Samir Lounis
abstract: Spin-momentum locking is widely regarded as a hallmark of relativistic spin-orbit coupling. Here we demonstrate analytically that it can instead emerge solely from magnetic chirality. Solving the minimal tight-binding model of electrons coupled to a spin spiral using a generalized Bloch theorem, we show that the spiral generates chirality-dependent p-wave magnetism characterized by the antisymmetric spin texture $\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{k})=-\boldsymbol{s}(-\boldsymbol{k})$. The exact solution further yields closed-form expressions for the electrical conductivity and the spin Edelstein susceptibility, revealing a microscopic mechanism by which magnetic chirality alone can generate spin polarization without spin-orbit coupling, with direct implications also for chirality-induced spin selectivity. In the strong exchange-coupling regime, the spin-dependent physics of the spin spiral becomes directly analogous to the orbital-dependent physics of electrons propagating through a non-magnetic helix. Our work establishes a minimal exactly solvable model of chirality-induced spin-momentum locking and spin-charge conversion beyond the conventional spin-orbit coupled paradigm.
summary: This theoretical work proves that magnetic chirality alone can induce spin-momentum locking and generate measurable spin polarization via the Edelstein effect, bypassing the need for intrinsic spin-orbit coupling. By solving a minimal tight-binding model for electrons coupled to a spin spiral, the authors derive exact expressions for transport properties. This establishes spin spirals as fundamental archetypes of chiral magnetism relevant for spintronics.
main_problem: To analytically demonstrate that spin-momentum locking and chirality-dependent p-wave magnetism can arise solely from magnetic chirality, bypassing the need for intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC).
main_result: The study derives closed-form expressions showing that a spin spiral generates measurable spin polarization via the Edelstein effect using only its magnetic chirality.
method: The authors solve the minimal tight-binding model exactly by employing a generalized Bloch theorem and transforming to a rotating spin frame of reference.
model_or_system: The system consists of conduction electrons coupled to a background forming a non-collinear spin spiral. The analysis uses a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating exchange coupling ($J$) and hopping ($t$).
key_observables: Electrical conductivity ($\sigma_{zz}$), chirality-dependent spin Edelstein susceptibility ($\chi^s_{z}$), and the resulting $p$-wave magnetism characterized by $\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{k}) = -\mathbf{s}(-\mathbf{k})$.
important_parameters: The relative strengths of hopping ($t$) versus exchange coupling ($J$), and the chirality parameter ($q$). The strong-coupling limit ($J \gg t$) is particularly analyzed.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving a minimal tight-binding model; initial interpretations are limited to weak coupling, though the full analysis accounts for band hybridization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic spin spirals with positive and negative chirality ($q>0$ vs $q<0$), showing how the effective field shifts bands. They also present numerical results for band structure, spin texture, conductivity, and Edelstein susceptibility in various coupling regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by setting up the model Hamiltonian, applying generalized Bloch theorems to solve the system exactly, deriving analytical expressions for transport coefficients ($\sigma$ and $\chi^s$), and finally establishing analogies between spin-spiral physics and orbital physics in non-magnetic helices.
why_interesting: It provides a fundamental mechanism for generating chiral electronic responses (like the Edelstein effect) purely from magnetic order, offering an alternative paradigm to SOC mechanisms often studied in AMO or condensed matter systems.
